blocks.text: Which serpents, moreover, sing back, or grow deaf at the chant, or whose poison is believed to be stronger than any spell, none of the Greeks explains. Except that Aelian, book 1, chapter 54, seems to assign this to the asp as its peculiar property, that against its bite neither medicines nor incantations are of any avail: Καὶ ἔχεως, he says, δῆγμα, καὶ ὄφεως, ἀλλ᾽ οὖν, φασὶν, ἀντιπάλων μὴ διαμαρτάνειν φαρμάκων. Καὶ τὰ μὲν αὐτῶν ἀκούω πόματα εἶναι, τὰ δὲ χρίσματα· καὶ ἐπῳδαὶ δὲ ἐπραΰναν τινῶν ἐγχεισθέντα ἰόν. Ἀσπίδος δὲ ἀκούω μόνον δῆγμα ἀνίατον εἶναι, καὶ ἐπικουρίας κρεῖττον. [Kai echeōs … dēgma, kai opheōs, all' oun, phasin, antipalōn mē diamartanein pharmakōn. Kai ta men autōn akouō pomata einai, ta de chrismata; kai epōdai de epraynan tinōn encheisthenta ion. Aspidos de akouō monon dēgma aniaton einai, kai epikourias kreitton.] The bites of the viper and of other serpents, they say, are not without remedies to be set against the evil. [col. 392] Of these I hear that some are given to drink, others are rubbed on; in some cases even incantations have mitigated the injected poison. But I have learned that the bite of the asp alone is incurable and beyond all help. But the matter, left untouched by the Greeks, is set out accurately and clearly by Avicenna, following the Arab philosophers, in the chapter On the species of serpents, which begins thus ^{e)}: ان العلما بامر الحيات وطبايعها قسموها ثلثة اقسام شديدة الحدة [inna al-ʿulamā bi-amr al-ḥayyāt wa-ṭabāyiʿihā qassamūhā thalathat aqsām shadīdat al-ḥidda] [III, 173] لا تمهل من الحال الي فوق ثلث ساعات ولا علاج للسوعها وهي الصم والاصلال ولا ينفع فيها الا قطع العضو في الحال او الكي البالع النافذ بالنار فانه يحرق السم ويضيق المجاري [lā tumhil min al-ḥāl ilī fawq thalath sāʿāt wa-lā ʿilāj li-lusūʿihā wa-hiya al-ṣumm wa-al-aṣlāl wa-lā yanfaʿ fīhā illā qaṭʿ al-ʿuḍw fī al-ḥāl aw al-kayy al-bāliʿ al-nāfidh bi-al-nār fa-innahu yaḥriq al-samm wa-yuḍayyiq al-majārī] The philosophers, in their books on serpents and their nature, divide them into three kinds. In the first species the force of the poison is so intense that death is not delayed beyond three hours from the time of the bite, nor is there any cure. For they are of the class of the deaf and the hissing (that is, as we have shown, of those which either seem to grow deaf at the chant, because they are no more affected by it than if they were deaf, or even τῷ ἐπαοιδῷ ἀντᾴδουσι [tō epaoidō antadousi], sing back to the charmer, so that the charm is ineffective against them). Therefore nothing helps except amputation of the limb at the same moment, or a burning that penetrates to the inmost parts; because it burns out the poison and constricts the passages. He adds that to this species belong الملكة [al-malika], the regulus, which kills by sight and hearing alone; and الخطاف [al-khaṭṭāf], the chelidonian asp; and الاسفيس اليابسة [al-asfīs al-yābisa], the dry asp, or χερσαίαν [chersaian]; of which the latter kills within three hours, the former within two; and البزاقة [al-bazzāqa], the ptyas asp, from which the bitten man perishes قبل ان توجع [qabl an tūjiʿ], before he feels pain, that is, he dies without pain; the Latin translator absurdly has before it returns, because he read ترجع [tarjiʿ] for توجع [tūjiʿ]. Of the same sort is that a little later the same translator places in this same class arched deaf ones, which multiply in the lands of Egypt. Arched deaf ones, that is, الصم المقوسة [al-ṣumm al-muqawwasa]. So he seems to have read, without any sense, instead of الصم المقعصة [al-ṣumm al-muqʿiṣa], which are deaf serpents that bring death swiftly. Of this kind, besides the regulus and the asp, are المقرنة [al-muqarrana], the cerastes, and اوبريس [ūbrīs], the hydrus, and كرسودروس [kursūdrūs], the chersydrus, all of which Avicenna counts among the deaf in what follows. Thus in the chapter On the basilisk: هو الاول من الصم [huwa al-awwal min al-ṣumm] It is the first of the deaf. And in the chapter On the chelidonian asp: وهي من الصم [wa-hiya min al-ṣumm] This too is of the deaf. And below: وعلاجها علاج الصم [wa-ʿilājuhā ʿilāj al-ṣumm] And its cure is the cure of the deaf. He says the same of the chersaean asp. And of the ptyas: علاجها من جنس علاج الصم [ʿilājuhā min jins ʿilāj al-ṣumm] It is cured in the same way as the deaf. And in the chapter On the cerastes: هي جنس من الصم [hiya jins min al-ṣumm] It is of the class of the [col. 393] deaf. And On the hydrus, or chersydrus: هي اصغر من الاصله صما [hiya aṣghar min al-aṣla ṣamman] It is smaller than the dryinus, deaf. So that it is now obscure to no one that the Arabs call deaf all serpents which they believe to be immune to incantation. Hence Alcamus says expressly: الاصم من الحية لا يقبل الرقي [al-aṣamm min al-ḥayya lā yaqbal al-ruqī] A deaf serpent is one [III, 174] which does not admit incantation. Such, moreover, they hold to be all those whose poison is intense in the highest degree, namely the regulus, asp, cerastes, hydrus, chersydrus. With this doctrine it will seem to agree that the royal Psalmist places the asp, and Jeremiah the regulus or basilisk, in that class. As if it were established by sure experience either that magicians never attempt to charm that kind of serpent, or, if they attempt it, that they succeed so little that it often even turns to the ruin of those who try.
